hypotheses.observation: The same immutable input tensor feeds an elementwise path and a row-wise reduction path at separated use sites, with one logical row mapped to one thread block.
hypotheses.mechanism: A fused row-level schedule can retain each thread's input elements across the reduction and normalization phases, avoiding a second global-memory read when resource usage permits.
hypotheses.transformation: Fuse the reduction and elementwise normalization work within the row block, staging the row values in registers or shared memory until the reduction result is available.
preconditions: The existing row-to-block mapping is retained.
The input values can be retained across the reduction without exceeding register or shared-memory limits.
A block-level synchronization and reduction scheme is available.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Potentially reduces global-memory traffic and may improve latency by reusing the immutable row values between separated uses.
risks: Retaining values may increase register pressure or shared-memory use and reduce occupancy.
Synchronization and staging overhead may offset the benefit.
Numerical behavior may change if reduction ordering changes.
unknowns: The size of the retained per-row data and available shared-memory capacity are UNKNOWN.
The current reduction ordering and numerical tolerance requirements are UNKNOWN.
required_evidence: Measure compiler-reported register usage and achieved occupancy for the fused schedule.
Measure global load traffic for the input tensor before and after fusion.
Verify numerical error against the required RMSNorm tolerance.

hypotheses.observation: The per-thread working set is small relative to the available execution context, while one logical row is assigned to one thread block.
hypotheses.mechanism: A row-block tiled implementation can cooperatively stage input values and perform the reduction using warp- or block-local data exchange, reducing repeated global-memory access and improving locality.
hypotheses.transformation: Organize each row block around cooperative loading into a compact tile, perform the row reduction locally, then apply the elementwise path from the staged tile.
preconditions: The row dimensions are compatible with cooperative block tiling.
The staged tile fits within the available shared-memory or register budget.
The block can synchronize safely between staging, reduction, and normalization.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Potentially improves data reuse and memory locality, with lower global-memory demand if the current graph reloads the input between use sites.
risks: Shared-memory staging can add latency and synchronization.
Bank conflicts or an unfavorable tile shape may reduce throughput.
The tile may not remain small for all supported row sizes.
unknowns: Whether the current implementation reloads the input between use sites is UNKNOWN.
The row width, access alignment, and tile shape are UNKNOWN.
Global traffic and memory-system bottlenecks are UNKNOWN.
required_evidence: Inspect or trace input loads to determine whether values are reloaded between the two uses.
Measure global load transactions and cache hit behavior.
Evaluate performance across representative row widths and alignments.

hypotheses.observation: The input is immutable between two uses and the per-thread working set is small, but register pressure and global traffic are explicitly unknown.
hypotheses.mechanism: A resource-adaptive schedule can choose between retaining the input in registers and using a lighter-weight reload or shared-memory path, avoiding a universal fusion choice that could harm occupancy.
hypotheses.transformation: Introduce a dispatch or specialization boundary based on row shape and resource estimates: use register retention when pressure is acceptable, otherwise use shared-memory staging or a controlled reload.
preconditions: Row-shape or launch-configuration information is available at dispatch time.
Resource estimates or compiled variants can distinguish acceptable register pressure.
All variants preserve the required reduction semantics.
hypotheses.expected_effect: May preserve reuse benefits for favorable shapes while limiting occupancy loss for shapes where retention is too expensive.
risks: Multiple variants increase maintenance and tuning complexity.
Dispatch overhead or misclassification can erase gains.
A reload path may increase global traffic.
unknowns: The threshold at which register retention reduces occupancy is UNKNOWN.
The relative cost of reload versus shared-memory staging is UNKNOWN.
The distribution of supported row shapes is UNKNOWN.
required_evidence: Collect register usage, occupancy, and execution time by row shape for each schedule variant.
Measure global traffic for register-retention, shared-memory, and reload variants.
Determine the supported row-shape distribution and dispatch overhead.
